Hi all — quick summary of what I pulled together from traces and telemetry (attached files: kv-cache-metrics.png, retry-trace.log):

Findings (initial):
- KV cache: pronounced thrash on ~3 hot prefixes (hit-rate dropped during the peak windows from ~78% to ~26%), likely because requests shifted to a small set of templates during the campaign. This increases token work per request.
- Worker concurrency: multiple workers hit the configured concurrency_cap of 64; in-flight requests per worker spiked and queued. The queueing time correlated with p99 increases.
- Retries: client observed 429s early in the ramp; subsequent naive retry behavior from the client produced short retry storms (bursts inside our servers) that magnified in-flight pressure.
- No obvious GC or OOM on workers; CPU utilization rose but stayed within acceptable ranges.

Hypothesis: a combo of hot-prefix cache thrash + client retry amplification pushed many workers to their concurrency ceiling. Queueing time increased and some requests timed out (524) when upstream kept sockets open waiting.

Recommended next actions (fast):
1) Approve temporary concurrency cap increase to 128 for FL-78 pool for 72 hours (monitor cost/frame) — expected immediate p99 relief.
2) Enable prefix caching for the 3 hot prefixes and pre-warm (should reduce token work per call).
3) Push a short client guidance note to FastLedger recommending exponential backoff and jitter for retries and reducing aggressive retry loops.
4) Add a temporary per-customer smoothing policy (limit short-window burst QPS) to avoid sharp ramps.

I'll push a trimmed set of traces to the shared drive and stand by to roll any runtime flags once we get approval. If we do the cap bump, let's watch p50/p95/p99 and the worker queue depth every 10m.

— Marissa
Sr. Reliability Engineer, Redwood Inference
